Sweating: central and preganglionic lesions cause facial anhidrosis; postganglionic lesions beyond the carotid bifurcation spare most of the face because sudomotor fibres follow the external carotid.
Mention pharmacological confirmation (e.g. apraclonidine or cocaine testing) as principle.
questions.modelAnswer:
Mrs Collins has a left Horner's syndrome with features of lower brachial plexus involvement. Together with the apical opacity, this strongly suggests a Pancoast tumour at the lung apex.

The sympathetic supply to the eye uses three neurons:
- First-order: hypothalamus, through the brainstem and cervical cord, to the ciliospinal centre at C8–T2.
- Second-order (preganglionic): leave through the T1 root and white ramus and climb the chain over the pleural dome, next to the lung apex, to the superior cervical ganglion. An apical tumour damages them here.
- Third-order (postganglionic): travel on the internal carotid through the cavernous sinus to the dilator pupillae (via long ciliary nerves) and the superior tarsal (Müller's) muscle.

Her features follow:
- Partial ptosis from paralysis of the superior tarsal muscle; levator (oculomotor) still works.
- Miosis from unopposed sphincter pupillae, most obvious in dim light when the normal pupil dilates.
- Shoulder and inner arm pain with weak small hand muscles from invasion of the C8–T1 roots or lower trunk.

A third nerve palsy is different. The ptosis is usually marked, because levator is paralysed. The pupil, if involved, is dilated, with the difference greatest in bright light. The eye lies down and out because only lateral rectus and superior oblique are working.

The pattern of sweating loss depends on the level. Central and preganglionic lesions, like hers, cause anhidrosis of the face on the same side. Sweat-gland fibres for most of the face leave the superior cervical ganglion with the external carotid artery. A postganglionic lesion on the internal carotid, such as a carotid dissection, therefore usually spares facial sweating apart from a small area of the forehead. The diagnosis can be confirmed with pharmacological eye-drop tests (cocaine or apraclonidine), and the lesion is located by imaging.

questions.q:
Mr Edward Lam, 71, a right-handed retired teacher, is admitted after a stroke. His speech is slow, halting and effortful, consisting mainly of nouns ('Wife... car... hospital'). He follows simple commands but struggles with complex grammatical instructions, cannot repeat phrases and is clearly frustrated. He has weakness of the right face and arm, with the leg less affected. Three months later, a different patient, Mrs Ruth Gold, 68, speaks fluently with frequent made-up words, cannot follow commands and seems unaware of her errors.

Localise each patient's lesion and vascular territory, explain the clinical features with reference to models of language, and evaluate the limitations of the classical model.
markScheme: Mr Lam: Broca's (non-fluent/expressive) aphasia — left inferior frontal gyrus (pars opercularis/triangularis) and surrounding area.
Superior division of left MCA; face and arm weakness from adjacent precentral gyrus, leg spared (ACA territory).
Features: telegraphic, agrammatic speech; relatively preserved comprehension but difficulty with complex syntax; impaired repetition; insight and frustration.
Mrs Gold: Wernicke's (fluent/receptive) aphasia — left posterior superior temporal gyrus.
Inferior division of left MCA; often no hemiparesis; may have right upper quadrantanopia (Meyer's loop).
Features: fluent paraphasic speech, neologisms, poor comprehension and repetition, reduced insight (anosognosia).
Wernicke–Geschwind model: Wernicke's area (comprehension) linked to Broca's area (production) via arcuate fasciculus; conduction aphasia predicted.
Limitations: lesions classically causing Broca's aphasia are usually larger than Broca's area; pure Broca's area lesions cause milder deficits.
Dual-stream model (Hickok and Poeppel): ventral stream (sound to meaning, temporal) and dorsal stream (sound to articulation, frontoparietal).
Comprehension in Broca's aphasia not entirely normal (syntactic comprehension impaired); language networks are distributed; individual variation and recovery/plasticity.
Clinical value of the classical model for bedside localisation despite limitations.
Structured, evaluative answer.
questions.modelAnswer:
Mr Lam has Broca's (non-fluent, expressive) aphasia. His speech is slow, effortful and telegraphic, made up mostly of nouns without grammatical words. He understands simple commands but not complex grammar, he cannot repeat, and his frustration shows he knows something is wrong. The lesion involves the left inferior frontal gyrus (pars opercularis and triangularis) and surrounding frontal cortex and white matter, in the territory of the superior division of the left middle cerebral artery. The neighbouring precentral gyrus face and arm areas are affected, while the leg area on the medial surface, supplied by the anterior cerebral artery, is relatively spared.

Mrs Gold has Wernicke's (fluent, receptive) aphasia. Her speech flows normally but is full of paraphasias and neologisms, her comprehension and repetition are poor, and she is unaware of her errors. The lesion is in the left posterior superior temporal gyrus, supplied by the inferior division of the left middle cerebral artery. Hemiparesis is often absent, but damage to Meyer's loop may cause a right upper quadrantanopia.

The Wernicke–Geschwind model explains these patterns. Wernicke's area decodes heard words into meaning, the arcuate fasciculus carries the information forward, and Broca's area plans articulation. The model correctly predicted conduction aphasia, in which repetition is lost while fluency and comprehension are kept.

The model has important limitations:
- Lasting Broca's aphasia usually needs damage well beyond Broca's area, including the insula and deep white matter. Lesions confined to Broca's area often cause only temporary deficits.
- Comprehension in Broca's aphasia is not normal. Grammatically complex sentences are misunderstood, suggesting the frontal cortex helps process syntax.
- Modern dual-stream models, such as Hickok and Poeppel's, describe a ventral temporal stream mapping sound to meaning, often involving both hemispheres, and a dorsal stream in the left hemisphere mapping sound to articulation. This fits better with imaging and lesion studies.
- Language depends on networks that vary between individuals and reorganise during recovery.

The classical syndromes remain useful for bedside localisation and for planning speech and language therapy, but they are simplifications of a distributed system.

questions.q:
Ms Chloe Martin, 26, has a history of depression and has been taking an SSRI for two years. After a dental procedure she is given tramadol for pain. Over the next day she becomes agitated, sweaty and tremulous, with a temperature of 38.6 °C, a heart rate of 124/min, dilated pupils, diarrhoea, brisk reflexes and inducible clonus that is most marked in the legs.

Explain the likely diagnosis and its mechanism. Discuss the pharmacology of serotonin at the synapse and the mechanisms of the drugs involved. Compare this with neuroleptic malignant syndrome and anticholinergic toxicity, explaining the features that distinguish them.
markScheme: Serotonin syndrome (serotonin toxicity) from SSRI plus tramadol.
Serotonin synthesised from tryptophan (tryptophan hydroxylase, rate-limiting), stored in vesicles, released, acts on multiple 5-HT receptors; action terminated by SERT reuptake and MAO-A breakdown.
SSRI: blocks SERT. Tramadol: weak μ-opioid agonist plus serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibition — additive serotonergic effect.
Excess 5-HT2A (and 5-HT1A) stimulation in CNS and periphery causes the triad.
Triad: neuromuscular hyperactivity (clonus, hyperreflexia, tremor, worse in lower limbs), autonomic instability (hyperthermia, tachycardia, sweating, mydriasis, diarrhoea), altered mental state.
Rapid onset (hours) after adding or increasing a serotonergic drug.
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome: dopamine D2 blockade or withdrawal of dopaminergic drugs; slower onset (days); lead-pipe rigidity, bradyreflexia, high fever, raised CK, reduced consciousness.
Anticholinergic toxicity: muscarinic blockade; dry hot skin (no sweating), urinary retention, reduced bowel sounds, mydriasis, normal reflexes, no clonus.
Management principles: stop serotonergic drugs, supportive cooling, benzodiazepines; 5-HT2A antagonist (cyproheptadine) as a mechanism-based option; no doses.
Mention other serotonergic interactions (MAOIs, linezolid, triptans, MDMA).
questions.modelAnswer:
Ms Martin has serotonin syndrome (serotonin toxicity), caused by adding tramadol to her SSRI. It developed within hours, and she shows all three parts of the classic triad. Neuromuscular hyperactivity appears as tremor, brisk reflexes and inducible clonus that is worse in the legs. Autonomic overactivity appears as fever, tachycardia, sweating, dilated pupils and diarrhoea. Her agitation is the change in mental state.

Serotonin is made from tryptophan, with tryptophan hydroxylase as the rate-limiting enzyme, and stored in vesicles. After release it acts on many 5-HT receptor subtypes, most G-protein coupled, with 5-HT3 being ionotropic. Its action ends mainly by reuptake through the serotonin transporter (SERT), followed by breakdown by monoamine oxidase A. SSRIs block SERT and raise synaptic serotonin. Tramadol is a weak μ-opioid agonist that also blocks reuptake of serotonin and noradrenaline. The two drugs therefore add together. Excess stimulation of 5-HT2A receptors, with a contribution from 5-HT1A, in the brainstem, spinal cord and periphery produces the syndrome. Other risky combinations involve MAO inhibitors, linezolid (which inhibits MAO), triptans in some settings, and MDMA.

Treatment is to stop the serotonergic drugs and give supportive care with cooling and fluids. Benzodiazepines control agitation and muscle overactivity. A 5-HT2A antagonist such as cyproheptadine is used in moderate cases, and severe hyperthermia needs intensive care.

Neuroleptic malignant syndrome follows D2 blockade by antipsychotics or abrupt withdrawal of dopaminergic drugs. It develops over days rather than hours. Its features are severe lead-pipe rigidity with slow movements and reduced reflexes rather than clonus, high fever, autonomic instability, reduced consciousness and a markedly raised creatine kinase.

Anticholinergic toxicity, caused by muscarinic blockade, also produces fever, tachycardia, dilated pupils and agitation or delirium. The skin, however, is hot, dry and flushed because sweat glands are cholinergic, and bowel sounds are reduced with urinary retention. Tone and reflexes are usually normal, with no clonus.

The key bedside distinctions are clonus and hyperreflexia (serotonin syndrome), rigidity and slow reflexes (neuroleptic malignant syndrome), and dry skin with normal reflexes (anticholinergic toxicity).

questions.q:
Mrs Margaret Dunn, 74, a retired librarian who lives alone and still drives, is brought to the emergency department by her daughter. That morning, while making breakfast, she had sudden weakness of the left arm and face with slurred speech, lasting about 40 minutes and fully resolving before arrival. She has hypertension and an irregularly irregular pulse. Examination is now normal. An ECG confirms atrial fibrillation.

Explain the likely diagnosis and the anatomical localisation of her symptoms. Describe how she should be assessed and managed according to current UK guidance, explaining the reasoning for each step, including secondary prevention.
markScheme: Transient ischaemic attack: transient focal neurological deficit with full resolution and no infarction on imaging (tissue-based definition).
Left face and arm weakness with dysarthria: right hemisphere, likely right MCA territory (or deep capsular region).
AF suggests cardioembolic source: thrombus from the left atrial appendage.
NICE NG128: aspirin immediately unless contraindicated (and no bleeding disorder/anticoagulant), refer for specialist assessment within 24 hours.
Risk scores such as ABCD2 are not recommended to determine urgency.
Imaging: MRI (diffusion-weighted) when needed to determine territory or exclude mimics; carotid imaging (duplex ultrasound) urgently.
Carotid endarterectomy for symptomatic stenosis (around 50–99% by NASCET) if appropriate.
AF: anticoagulation (DOAC, a direct factor Xa or thrombin inhibitor) for secondary prevention once haemorrhage excluded; balance bleeding risk.
Other secondary prevention: statin, blood pressure control, lifestyle (smoking, diet, exercise), driving advice (no driving for 1 month after TIA for car licence holders).
Explains mechanisms: antiplatelet vs anticoagulant reasoning (AF clots fibrin-rich).
questions.modelAnswer:
Mrs Dunn has had a transient ischaemic attack. This is a short episode of focal neurological dysfunction caused by ischaemia that resolves completely and, under the tissue-based definition, leaves no infarct on imaging. Weakness of the left face and arm with dysarthria points to the right hemisphere. The likely site is the right middle cerebral artery territory, which covers the face and arm motor areas, or the deep fibres of the internal capsule supplied by its lenticulostriate branches. Her atrial fibrillation makes a cardioembolic cause likely: thrombus forms in the poorly contracting left atrial appendage and travels to the brain.

Under NICE guideline NG128, she should be given aspirin straight away, unless contraindicated, and referred for specialist assessment within 24 hours of symptom onset. Risk-scoring tools such as ABCD2 are no longer recommended for deciding urgency, because they do not reliably identify who will have a stroke. All suspected TIAs are treated as urgent.

The specialist assessment includes:
- Brain imaging where it will change management. MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging is preferred to confirm the territory and exclude mimics or haemorrhage.
- Urgent carotid imaging. Although AF is a likely cause, a symptomatic right internal carotid stenosis would also need treatment. A significant symptomatic stenosis (around 50–99% by NASCET criteria) should be considered for urgent carotid endarterectomy.
- Blood tests, including glucose, lipids and a full blood count.

For secondary prevention, long-term anticoagulation is better than antiplatelet therapy for clots arising in AF, which are fibrin-rich and form in slow-flowing blood. A direct oral anticoagulant (a factor Xa or thrombin inhibitor) is usually chosen once haemorrhage has been excluded, weighing stroke risk against bleeding risk. Aspirin is not used long-term alongside it without a specific reason.

Other measures are a high-intensity statin, blood pressure control, stopping smoking, and diet and exercise advice. She must also receive driving advice: car drivers should not drive for one month after a TIA. Diabetes, if present, should be managed.

questions.q:
Mr Simon Ford, 45, a company director, is brought to clinic by his wife. Over two years he has become rude and tactless, made inappropriate sexual comments to staff, overeaten sweet foods and spent money impulsively. He seems unconcerned about these changes. He can still find his way around, recalls recent events reasonably well and scores near normal on a brief memory test, but he struggles to plan tasks, cannot switch between rules on a card-sorting test and gives very few words beginning with 'F' in one minute. His father developed a similar illness in his fifties.

Localise the likely pathology, explain how each feature relates to frontal lobe function, and discuss how you would distinguish this from Alzheimer's disease.
markScheme: Likely behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia, affecting orbitofrontal/ventromedial and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (and anterior temporal lobes).
Disinhibition, tactlessness and inappropriate sexual comments: orbitofrontal/ventromedial prefrontal damage (impaired social conduct and inhibition).
Apathy or lack of concern (loss of insight): medial frontal and anterior cingulate involvement.
Hyperorality/dietary change (sweet foods): orbitofrontal and insular involvement.
Impaired planning, poor set-shifting (card sorting, e.g. Wisconsin) and reduced letter fluency: dorsolateral prefrontal executive dysfunction.
Relative preservation of episodic memory and visuospatial skills early (hippocampus and parietal lobes relatively spared).
Family history suggests a genetic form (e.g. C9orf72, MAPT, GRN mutations).
Alzheimer's disease typically begins with episodic memory loss (hippocampal/entorhinal), later parietal visuospatial problems; usually later onset.
Imaging: frontal and anterior temporal atrophy (MRI) or hypometabolism (FDG-PET) versus medial temporal/parietal changes in Alzheimer's.
Brief memory screens may be near normal in early frontotemporal dementia, so behavioural history from an informant is crucial.
questions.modelAnswer:
Mr Ford's early-onset change in personality and behaviour, with executive impairment, preserved memory and a family history, suggests behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia. This affects the orbitofrontal, ventromedial and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, the anterior cingulate and insula, and often the anterior temporal lobes.

Each feature maps onto frontal function:
- Disinhibition, tactlessness and inappropriate sexual remarks reflect orbitofrontal and ventromedial damage. These areas link emotional value to behaviour and hold back socially inappropriate responses, as the case of Phineas Gage first suggested.
- His lack of concern reflects loss of insight and empathy, linked to medial frontal, anterior cingulate and right-sided frontoinsular degeneration.
- Overeating sweet foods (hyperorality) is linked to orbitofrontal and insular involvement in reward and appetite.
- Poor planning, inability to switch rules on card sorting (perseveration) and reduced letter fluency are dysexecutive features of dorsolateral prefrontal dysfunction.
- Impulsive spending combines disinhibition with poor judgement.

Memory and spatial skills are relatively preserved early because the hippocampus and parietal lobes are spared at first. This is why brief memory screens may look nearly normal, and an informant's account of behaviour is essential. The family history suggests a genetic form, such as a C9orf72 repeat expansion or a MAPT or GRN mutation, and genetic counselling should be offered.

Alzheimer's disease usually starts later and with episodic memory loss, reflecting early involvement of the entorhinal cortex and hippocampus, followed by word-finding and visuospatial problems as the temporoparietal cortex is affected. Personality is relatively preserved early. MRI in frontotemporal dementia shows frontal and anterior temporal atrophy, often asymmetric, whereas Alzheimer's disease shows medial temporal and parietal atrophy. FDG-PET hypometabolism follows the same patterns, and CSF or PET markers of amyloid and tau support Alzheimer's disease.

questions.q: 'Parkinson's disease is best understood not as a disorder of dopamine, but as a disorder of the whole nervous system.' Critically evaluate this statement, drawing on the pathology, clinical features, circuit physiology and treatment of Parkinson's disease.
markScheme: Classic view: degeneration of substantia nigra pars compacta dopaminergic neurons; motor features (bradykinesia, rigidity, rest tremor) appear after substantial loss of nigral neurons/striatal dopamine.
Circuit model: reduced direct pathway and increased indirect pathway activity raise GPi/SNr output and inhibit the thalamus; abnormal beta oscillations.
Dopamine replacement (levodopa, agonists, MAO-B and COMT inhibitors) is effective for motor symptoms, supporting the dopamine model.
α-synuclein pathology (Lewy bodies) spreads beyond the nigra; Braak staging begins in the olfactory bulb and dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus.
Non-motor features: reduced sense of smell, REM sleep behaviour disorder, constipation, autonomic failure (orthostatic hypotension), depression, anxiety, cognitive decline/dementia, pain.
Non-dopaminergic systems involved: noradrenergic locus coeruleus, serotonergic raphe, cholinergic nucleus basalis; enteric and cardiac sympathetic nerves.
Levodopa-resistant features (gait freezing, postural instability, dementia, dysautonomia) show limits of dopamine-centric treatment.
Deep brain stimulation (subthalamic nucleus or GPi) shows circuit-level understanding.
Gut–brain hypothesis and evidence for and against (e.g. not all cases fit Braak staging).
Genetic forms (SNCA, LRRK2, GBA, PRKN) show heterogeneity.
Balanced conclusion: dopamine is central to motor features and treatment, but the disease is multisystem.
Structure, critical depth and use of evidence.
questions.modelAnswer:
The statement is broadly right, but it sets up a false choice. Dopamine loss is still central to the motor disease and its treatment, even though the pathology and symptoms reach well beyond it.

The classical account is strong. The cardinal motor signs (bradykinesia, rigidity and rest tremor) appear after substantial loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta. In the basal ganglia model, less dopamine weakens the D1 direct pathway and releases the D2 indirect pathway. Output from the internal globus pallidus rises and the motor thalamus is held back, and recordings show abnormal synchronised beta oscillations. The model is supported by the dramatic response to dopamine replacement with levodopa, dopamine agonists and MAO-B and COMT inhibitors. It also underpins deep brain stimulation.

The disease, however, extends far past the nigra:
- Lewy pathology made of α-synuclein appears in many places. Braak's staging proposes that it starts in the olfactory bulb and the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus and only later reaches the midbrain and cortex.
- Non-motor features often come years before diagnosis: reduced sense of smell, REM sleep behaviour disorder, constipation and depression.
- Autonomic failure, including orthostatic hypotension, reflects damage to peripheral sympathetic and enteric neurons.
- Other transmitter systems are affected: the noradrenergic locus coeruleus, serotonergic raphe nuclei and cholinergic nucleus basalis. These contribute to depression, anxiety, apathy and dementia.
- Disabling late problems such as freezing, postural instability, dementia and dysautonomia respond poorly to levodopa.

There are reasons for caution. Braak staging does not fit every patient, and 'brain-first' and 'body-first' subtypes have been proposed. Genetic forms involving SNCA, LRRK2, GBA1 and PRKN differ in their pathology; some PRKN cases lack Lewy bodies. 'Parkinson's disease' may therefore be several disorders sharing a dopaminergic endpoint.

In conclusion, Parkinson's disease is best seen as a multisystem α-synuclein disorder in which nigrostriatal dopamine loss produces the defining motor syndrome. Dopamine explains much of the diagnosis and early treatment. Understanding the wider nervous system is needed to explain the non-motor burden, disease progression and the search for disease-modifying treatments.

questions.q: 'Long-term potentiation is the cellular basis of learning and memory.' Critically evaluate this proposition with reference to the mechanisms of synaptic plasticity and the experimental evidence linking it to behaviour.
markScheme: Definition: LTP is a long-lasting increase in synaptic strength after high-frequency or patterned stimulation; first described in the hippocampus by Bliss and Lømo (1973).
Properties matching memory: input specificity, associativity, cooperativity, persistence.
Mechanism: NMDA receptors act as coincidence detectors (glutamate plus depolarisation to expel Mg²⁺); Ca²⁺ influx activates CaMKII and other kinases.
Early LTP: AMPA receptor phosphorylation and insertion; late LTP requires gene transcription and protein synthesis (CREB) and structural spine changes.
Hebbian principle: neurons that fire together strengthen connections.
LTD as a complementary mechanism; both needed for flexible encoding.
Evidence: NMDA antagonist (AP5) blocks spatial learning in the Morris water maze (Morris et al., 1986).
Genetic evidence: knockout of hippocampal NMDA receptor subunits impairs LTP and spatial memory; occlusion and saturation experiments.
Learning induces LTP-like changes (e.g. Whitlock et al., 2006 inhibitory avoidance in hippocampal CA1).

Limitations: correlation vs causation; some learning occurs despite impaired LTP; multiple forms of plasticity (intrinsic excitability, structural, neurogenesis); memory as systems-level consolidation.
Non-hippocampal memory (cerebellar LTD for motor learning, amygdala LTP for fear conditioning).
Balanced conclusion with structured argument.
questions.modelAnswer:
Long-term potentiation (LTP) is a lasting increase in synaptic strength after brief, high-frequency or patterned activity. Bliss and Lømo described it in the rabbit hippocampus in 1973. It fits Hebb's idea that connections between neurons that fire together grow stronger. It is the best-supported cellular mechanism for memory storage, but calling it 'the' basis of learning and memory is too strong.

At Schaffer collateral–CA1 synapses, LTP depends on NMDA receptors, which act as coincidence detectors. They conduct only when glutamate is bound and the postsynaptic membrane is depolarised enough to expel Mg²⁺. The resulting Ca²⁺ entry activates CaMKII and other kinases, which phosphorylate AMPA receptors and insert more of them into the membrane (early LTP). Late LTP needs gene transcription through CREB, new protein synthesis and enlargement of dendritic spines. Long-term depression (LTD), triggered by smaller, prolonged rises in Ca²⁺, weakens synapses and allows memories to be refined.

LTP is input-specific, associative and long-lasting, all properties that suit memory.

The evidence linking LTP to behaviour is substantial:
- Morris and colleagues (1986) showed that blocking NMDA receptors in the hippocampus with AP5 prevented LTP and impaired spatial learning in the water maze.
- Mice lacking NMDA receptors in CA1 lose both LTP and spatial memory.
- Whitlock and colleagues (2006) found that one-trial avoidance learning produced LTP-like changes in CA1 that partly occluded later electrically induced LTP. This suggests learning uses the same mechanism.
- Similar plasticity in the amygdala supports fear conditioning.

There are important limits. Much of the evidence is correlational, NMDA blockade also affects sensorimotor function, and pre-trained animals can learn new mazes despite it. Other mechanisms contribute too: changes in intrinsic excitability, structural remodelling, adult neurogenesis and cerebellar LTD for motor learning. Memory also depends on systems-level processes, such as the hippocampus gradually transferring memories to neocortex, which no single synaptic mechanism explains.

LTP is best regarded as a central and well-evidenced mechanism by which experience changes synapses. Memory, however, emerges from many forms of plasticity working within distributed circuits.

questions.q:
Mr Daniel Kerr, 52, has had Parkinson's disease for 9 years. His motor symptoms were initially well controlled with levodopa (with a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor), but he now experiences 'wearing off' before each dose, sudden 'off' periods, and writhing involuntary movements at peak dose. A dopamine agonist was added two years ago, after which his wife reports he has spent large sums gambling online. He has also developed vivid visual hallucinations at night.

Explain the pharmacological basis of each problem and discuss the options for managing them, focusing on mechanisms of action rather than doses.
markScheme: Levodopa crosses the BBB via the large neutral amino acid transporter; converted to dopamine by AADC; peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor (carbidopa/benserazide) increases CNS delivery.
Short plasma half-life; early disease buffered by surviving nigral terminals storing and releasing dopamine.
Wearing off: progressive terminal loss reduces storage, so striatal dopamine tracks plasma levodopa — shortened benefit.
Sudden 'on-off': erratic absorption (gastric emptying, dietary protein competition) and pulsatile stimulation.
Peak-dose dyskinesia: pulsatile stimulation of sensitised postsynaptic receptors, maladaptive plasticity in striatal pathways.
Impulse control disorder: dopamine agonists (particularly D3-preferring) overstimulate mesolimbic reward circuits; risk factors include younger age, male sex.
Hallucinations: dopaminergic overstimulation of mesolimbic/cortical pathways, plus disease progression (cortical Lewy pathology, cholinergic deficit).
Management of wearing off: smaller more frequent doses, MAO-B inhibitor, COMT inhibitor (prolong levodopa action), modified-release preparations.
Dyskinesia: reduce peak levodopa dose; amantadine (NMDA antagonism) as an option.
ICD: reduce/stop dopamine agonist (gradually, watch for dopamine agonist withdrawal syndrome), counselling, involve family.

Hallucinations: review medications (reduce agonist/anticholinergics), treat triggers; if needed antipsychotic with low D2 affinity (e.g. quetiapine, clozapine with monitoring); avoid typical antipsychotics.
Advanced therapies: continuous delivery (apomorphine infusion, levodopa–carbidopa intestinal gel, subcutaneous levodopa) or deep brain stimulation for selected patients.
questions.modelAnswer:
Levodopa crosses the blood–brain barrier on the large neutral amino acid transporter and is converted to dopamine by aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase; a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor increases central delivery and reduces nausea. Its half-life is short, but in early disease surviving nigral terminals store and release dopamine steadily, smoothing the response.

As terminals are lost, this buffer disappears and striatal dopamine follows plasma levodopa levels:
- Wearing off: each dose's benefit fades before the next one is due.
- Sudden 'off' periods: absorption is erratic, for example from delayed gastric emptying or competition from dietary protein for transport.
- Peak-dose dyskinesia: pulsatile, non-physiological stimulation of sensitised postsynaptic receptors causes maladaptive plasticity in the striatum, so high peaks produce involuntary movements.

Dopamine agonists, particularly those with strong D3 activity, stimulate mesolimbic reward circuits and are linked to impulse control disorders, including gambling, compulsive shopping and hypersexuality. Younger age and male sex are risk factors. His hallucinations reflect both dopaminergic overstimulation and disease progression, with cortical Lewy pathology and cholinergic loss, and raise the possibility of developing dementia.

Management should be led by a specialist and based on mechanism:
- Wearing off: give levodopa more often in smaller doses, or use modified-release forms. Add a MAO-B inhibitor or a COMT inhibitor (such as entacapone or opicapone) to slow dopamine and levodopa breakdown and prolong each dose.
- Dyskinesia: lower peak doses while keeping total cover. Amantadine, which blocks NMDA receptors, can reduce dyskinesia.
- Impulse control disorder: reduce and ideally stop the dopamine agonist gradually, watching for dopamine agonist withdrawal syndrome. Involve his wife and arrange financial safeguards and counselling.
- Hallucinations: simplify medication, look for infection and assess cognition. If they persist, a low-D2-affinity antipsychotic (quetiapine, or clozapine with blood monitoring) may be used; typical D2 antagonists must be avoided.
- Continuous stimulation (apomorphine infusion, intestinal levodopa gel or subcutaneous levodopa) smooths fluctuations. Deep brain stimulation suits selected patients without significant cognitive or psychiatric problems, so his hallucinations need assessing first.
